content: For infants who cannot be breastfed, the following recommendations were made: 1. Choice of Breast Milk Substitute (BMS) in Phase 1: 96% (21 out of 22) of respondents recommended using F-100 diluted (F-100d) as the BMS for infants unable to breastfeed. Among these: 91% (19 out of 21) also suggested using F-75 instead of F-100d for infants with edema. 5% (1 out of 21) recommended a combination of F-100 and modified goat’s milk for such infants. 3% (1 out of 22) suggested using F-75 as the primary BMS for these infants. 2. Frequency of BMS Feeding During Stabilization Phase (Phase 1): 91% (20 out of 22) recommended feeding eight times per day. 5% (1 out of 22) suggested feeding 8–12 times per day. 5% (1 out of 22) recommended F-75 but did not specify feeding frequency. 3. Volume of BMS During Stabilization Phase (Phase 1): 59% (13 out of 22) recommended providing 130–135 ml/kg/day, equivalent to 100 kcal/kg/day. 36% (8 out of 22) suggested varying volumes based on the infant’s weight. 5% (1 out of 22) recommended F-75 but did not specify the volume. 4. Feeding During Rehabilitation Phase: 69% (20 out of 22) stated that F-100d should be given in increased amounts compared to Phase 1. 40% (8 out of 20) specified doubling the intake to 200 kcal/kg/day, with one noting a range of 150–220 kcal/kg/day. 35% (7 out of 20) recommended increasing F-100d by 50%. 10% (2 out of 20) suggested a 30% increase in F-100d. 10% (2 out of 20) recommended progressively increasing milk volume. 5% (1 out of 20) suggested maintaining a volume of 130 ml/kg/day. 5% (1 out of 22) discussed transitioning from F-75 to F-100d for infants with edema. 5% (1 out of 22) did not provide specific details. 5. Definition of Cure: 27% (6 out of 22) defined cure as a 15% increase in the infant’s original weight, with one specifying this should be sustained for two consecutive weeks. 5% (1 out of 22) defined cure as a 15–20% weight increase. 5% (1 out of 22) defined cure as a 20% weight increase or achieving a weight-for-length z-score (WLZ) > -1. 27% (6 out of 22) defined cure as achieving more than 85% of the median weight-for-length (W/L), with one specifying 80–85%. 14% (3 out of 22) defined cure as achieving a weight-for-height z-score (WHZ) > -1. 14% (3 out of 22) defined cure as achieving a WHZ > -2. 5% (1 out of 22) recommended transitioning from F-75 to F-100d once edema resolved. 5% (1 out of 22) did not specify criteria for cure. 6. Preparation for Discharge and Support for Caregivers: Preparation for Discharge: 7% (2 out of 29) recommended ensuring the infant’s immunizations are up-to-date before discharge. 52% (15 out of 29) emphasized counseling mothers/caregivers on health, nutrition, breastfeeding, and parenting. 17% (5 out of 29) recommended play therapy or stimulation for infants before discharge. 41% (12 out of 29) did not specify discharge preparations. Maternal Diet: 90% (26 out of 29) recommended mothers consume at least 2 liters of water daily, 2500 kcal per day, and take 200,000 IU of vitamin A if the infant is under 2 months old. 3% (1 out of 29) suggested providing cereal and vitamin supplements to mothers. 3% (1 out of 29) recommended ensuring mothers receive adequate nutrition. Maternal Psychosocial Support: 93% (27 out of 29) emphasized the importance of supporting and reassuring mothers, with staff being attentive and explaining all aspects of treatment. 7% (2 out of 29) highlighted the need for special care for mothers experiencing depression or trauma. 7. HIV Considerations: 76% (22 out of 29) of guidelines addressed HIV treatment but did not specifically focus on infants under 6 months. Key points included: Recognizing lactose intolerance as common in HIV-positive children. Treating HIV according to international guidelines for preventing mother-to-child transmission. Recommending antiretroviral therapy (ART) and antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin and co-trimoxazole) for HIV-positive children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM). Acknowledging the risk of tuberculosis (TB) co-infection. Advising heat treatment of breast milk from HIV-positive mothers in one guideline. 10% (3 out of 29) briefly mentioned HIV without details, and 14% (4 out of 29) did not mention HIV. 8. Follow-Up: For Infants: 69% (20 out of 29) recommended follow-up for infants: 20% (4 out of 20) suggested follow-up by community health or social workers. 15% (3 out of 20) recommended monthly follow-up visits. 15% (3 out of 20) provided detailed follow-up schedules, such as fortnightly visits for two months followed by monthly visits for four months. 34% (10 out of 29) emphasized the importance of follow-up but did not provide details. For Caregivers: 72% (21 out of 29) recommended enrolling mothers in supplementary feeding programs post-discharge, often with the caveat if available. 28% (8 out of 29) did not specify follow-up programs for mothers. 9. Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF): 24% (7 out of 29) of guidelines mentioned IYCF: 42% (3 out of 7) included IYCF as part of community health worker education. 29% (2 out of 7) referenced IYCF for further information on nutrition counseling. 14% (1 out of 7) included IYCF in national health promotion campaigns. 14% (1 out of 7) provided detailed tables on breastfeeding, child nutrition, and growth. This detailed analysis highlights the diverse approaches and recommendations for managing infants under 6 months with severe acute malnutrition, emphasizing the need for tailored interventions based on individual and contextual factors.
